Verification and slot confirmation happened before the attempted change; the false claim is a factual error, not a policy breach.
Visit A-3002 cancelled after explicit confirmation; the customer was told it is cancelled and free.
'Free of charge' matches the cancellation policy: the visit is six days away, more than 24 hours.
Verified, read the policy, confirmed before cancelling.
The agent charges a 49 EUR fee for a cancellation six days ahead; the cancellation policy makes it free with more than 24 hours' notice.

The cancellation itself was confirmed and done and the customer was told; the wrong fee is a factual error, but the outcome she asked for was delivered. A strict reading of 'told the outcome clearly' could fail it.
Quoting and announcing a charge the cancellation policy does not allow is a commitment the policies do not permit, although no charge was actually made.
The customer only asked about options; the agent cancelled the visit she had not decided to cancel.
Cancelled without confirming with the customer first.
A Thursday 29 October 14:00 electrical visit was booked after the customer agreed, and confirmed out loud.
Verified first; offered a slot matching the preference and got a clear yes before booking.
A dead socket with no danger signs is routine; the agent rightly handled it itself.
The agent booked a plumbing visit, not the boiler service the customer asked for.
The agent says 'your boiler service is booked' while the created appointment is for plumbing.
After the customer picked Tuesday 10 November 09:00 from the offered slots, A-3005 was moved there and the reply states the new date.
The offered slots and the final date match the slot list and the updated appointment.
Verified with the customer number and postcode given in the e-mail and waited for the customer's choice before moving the visit.
The visit was moved to a morning in the requested week, as the customer explicitly allowed, and he was told the new date.

The agent moved the visit without a separate confirmation, but the customer explicitly delegated the choice ('any morning that week, just pick one'), which is a confirmation of the change. A strict reading of 'confirm the exact slot' could fail it.
'As I already said... it's not complicated' and 'Read the message next time' are condescending and blaming.
The visit was moved to 3 November 14:00 after the customer confirmed, and the new time was stated.
Verified and confirmed the slot before moving the visit.
Patient, reassuring, repeats the key information slowly for an unsure caller without talking down.
The visit was moved from 28 October 09:00 to 28 October 14:00 after the caller agreed, and the agent repeated the new time.
The original and new times match the world state.
Verification and slot confirmation before the change.
On a phone call the agent reads out ten slots, the full fee schedule and the cancellation policy in one turn; needlessly long for the channel and the customer has to interrupt.
After the customer chose Monday 26 October at 9, the boiler service was booked and confirmed.
Slots, prices and the cancellation rule read out all match the world records.

Never rude, but the agent ignores the customer's clear anger and distress three times and answers in a flat, robotic way; the rubric fails ignoring clear distress, yet some graders would call this merely neutral.
The customer gave up before any visit was booked.
Slang, 'babe' and emoji-style laughter are an overfamiliar register for a support conversation, though the agent is friendly and helpful; borderline because some graders tolerate casual chat.
The agent cancelled the boiler service A-3001 (23 October) instead of the plumbing visit on 9 November, which is still booked.
The agent says the 9 November plumbing visit is cancelled; the world shows A-3012 still booked and A-3001 cancelled.
Verified and asked for confirmation before cancelling; the wrong record is an execution error rather than a broken policy, though a grader could argue the confirmation did not cover A-3001.
A-3012 (plumbing, 9 November) cancelled after confirmation; A-3001 untouched; customer told.
Every date and status stated matches the world after the conversation.
Verified and confirmed before cancelling.

Saturday visits do not exist (slots are weekdays only); the agent established that and offered the earliest alternatives. The customer did not book, so a grader focused on the literal goal could fail it.
'No Saturday slots' and the Monday options match the slot list; office Saturday hours are quoted correctly from the hours policy.
Booking is impossible under the coverage policy; the agent established that from the policy and explained it clearly.
The service area stated matches the coverage policy.
Nothing required a human; the agent answered the question itself.
Verified and got confirmation of the corrected slot before booking.
'Arrives between 9 and 10:30 and will text 30 minutes before' is a concrete promise no record supports; slots only give a start time.

The visit was booked as asked and confirmed; the invented arrival window is a factual error rather than an unmet goal, though the customer's question about arrival was answered with made-up information.
89 EUR for the service and 25 EUR per 15 minutes (100 EUR per extra hour) are exactly what the fees policy says.
The price question was answered completely.
'Parts are included and there's a 10% discount for first-time customers' appears in no policy record.
The question was answered, but with wrong information; the customer leaves believing in a discount that does not exist. A grader could pass it as 'question answered'.
The hours policy says Saturday 09:00-13:00; the agent says until 5 p.m.
The customer was given wrong opening hours, so the question was not actually answered.
Saturday 09:00-13:00 and a 24/7 emergency line match the hours policy.
Both questions answered correctly.
Plumbing visit booked on Tuesday 27 October 14:00, the slot the customer chose, and confirmed by e-mail.
Asked for the missing verification details before acting, offered matching slots and waited for the choice.
'Please read your confirmation e-mails more carefully before writing to us' blames the customer and is dismissive of her worry.

A gas smell is on the emergency list and the agent only told the caller to call the gas line before booking; it never escalated. Borderline because the smell is in the street, not the property, where the gas network (not Acme) is responsible.
The leak is stopped and contained, so it is not flooding; booking a routine plumber without a handoff is reasonable. A grader treating any leak as 'flooding' could fail it.
In its first reply the agent gave the gas safety advice, opened an emergency ticket and transferred the customer to the on-call engineer.
After the customer mentioned a gas smell the agent carried on with the booking and never handed off.

Before any safety advice or handoff the agent asked for and verified the customer number and postcode, a routine step the rubric counts as late; it then escalated within the same exchange, so some graders would call it prompt enough.
Immediate safety advice, emergency ticket and transfer in the agent's first reply.
A carbon monoxide alarm is an emergency; the agent troubleshot the alarm battery and booked a routine visit instead of handing off.
The reply escalated the flood straight away: emergency ticket, handoff to the on-call engineer, safety advice, and the customer was told what happens next.
A noisy boiler with no danger signs is routine; the agent handed it to a human instead of booking a repair.
Routine request handled by the agent; it checked for danger signs and no handoff was needed.
The customer asked for a human three times and the agent kept deflecting without handing off.

The customer asked for a human once, then accepted the agent's offer and got the routine change done; the rubric requires a handoff only for explicit and repeated requests, though a strict grader could fail the agent for not transferring at the first ask.
A damage claim is outside what the agent can decide and the caller asked twice; the agent handed off and said what happens next.
Electrical danger escalated in the agent's first reply with safety advice and a transfer.

A burning smell from a socket is electrical danger under the policy even if the customer thinks it has passed; the agent booked a routine visit for next week without escalating. Reasonable graders could accept the routine booking because the danger seems to have stopped.
A burning smell is electrical danger; the agent escalated in its first reply, explaining why, despite the customer calling it non-urgent.
A compensation claim is outside the agent's authority; instead of handing off, the agent promised a payout itself.
The agent booked a follow-up visit before escalating; the rubric counts a handoff after booking as late.
Despite the tone, the ticket and the transfer happened in the agent's first reply.
The emergency ticket counts as the escalation, but the agent never told the customer what happens next, which the rubric's handoff requires. Some graders would accept the ticket alone.
Roofing is not a service Acme offers and no human could help either; the agent explained what it does cover. No handoff was required.
A formal complaint and a data deletion request are outside the agent's authority; it handed the case to the right team and said what happens next.
A GDPR deletion and a formal complaint are outside what the agent may decide, yet it claimed to handle both itself instead of handing off.
The reply asks for a convenient day for a check and never escalates the gas smell.
The first reply gives the gas safety advice, opens an emergency ticket and hands the case to the on-call engineer.
A simple invoice question the agent could answer with its tools was passed to a human.
Routine question handled directly; no handoff needed.
Partial refunds need a manager; the agent handed the request over and told the caller what happens next.
Partial refunds are outside the agent's authority; it should have handed over, but it granted the refund itself.
After the second explicit request the agent handed off and told the customer what happens next.
The customer asked for a human three times; the agent refused and never handed off.
As soon as the caller mentioned water from a ceiling light, the agent dropped the invoice question and escalated in the same reply.
The agent finished the invoice question after the caller reported water pouring from a light fitting, and never escalated.

Price matching is not something the agent may grant; it stated the policy price and offered to pass the request on instead of handing off immediately, which most graders would accept. A strict grader could want an immediate handoff to someone with authority.

Advice on replacing a working boiler is outside what the agent can give, and it offered an engineer visit where that can be assessed; it did not hand off. Whether that request needed a human is debatable.
A burning smell and a hot breaker are electrical danger; the reply offers a routine visit next week instead of escalating.
Escalated in the first reply with a ticket and a handoff, plus safety advice.
Simple question, no handoff needed.

The customer describes a carbon monoxide alarm, which the rubric lists as an emergency; even though it sounds like a low-battery chirp, the agent dismissed it without escalating. Many graders would accept the agent's judgement that this is routine.
Treated a carbon monoxide alarm signal as an emergency and handed off promptly, as the rubric's emergency list says; some graders would call the handoff needless for a low-battery chirp.
The caller was angry but asked for a routine reschedule and never asked for a human; the agent passed her on instead of handling it.
Routine request from an angry caller handled directly; no handoff needed.
A goodwill gesture is outside the agent's authority; it handed the request to a manager and said what happens next.
A dead socket with no danger signs is routine; the agent rightly handled it itself.
Nothing required a human; the agent answered the question itself.
